prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought the measurement of time to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18.

statement.case_for: I keep B009 with Katori and Ye as a single part, and my position has not changed in substance since round 1. What the exchange has done is let me test it against the chair's questions. On discovery versus instrument: the magic-wavelength condition is a statement about atomic polarisabilities at a specific wavelength, a physical insight that removes the dominant systematic of a trapped-atom clock and so permits interrogation of many atoms at once. That is where the statistical power behind 1e-18 comes from, and it is a different idea from the comb (2005) or from single-ion control (2012). On delivered consequences, which Danielsson and the chair press: the strongest delivered result I can cite is the resolution of the gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale height differences within one atomic ensemble, together with clock intercomparisons that already bound variation of fundamental constants and certain dark-matter couplings. Those are limits on nature, not only a better ruler. Dark-matter discovery and geodesy applications remain prospective, and I would not claim otherwise. On citation wording, I would anchor it on the invention and realisation and on the 1e-18 level as a stated achievement, not as a record that others may exceed, and I would put the magic-wavelength lattice in the text because it names precisely what is credited to Katori; Ye's part is the realisation to that accuracy and the move to many-body clock operation. On timing, the redefinition of the second is a consumer of these clocks, not a precondition for recognising the invention; I would not wait for it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains category and cumulative weight. Atomic precision measurement has been recognised in 2005 and 2012, and a reasonable colleague can judge that a third award from this lineage in two decades is too much, or that metrology does not meet a discovery standard however well reproduced. I also cannot make the credit airtight: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups produced decisive accuracy and comparison milestones, and Gill and the ion-clock lineage sit nearby. A two-name citation cannot honour them, and the committee should be honest that this is a limit of the three-person rule, not a sign that the history is simple. If the committee ruled that this year's prize must open a new scientific question rather than sharpen a measurement, as Eriksson says he would, B009 would fall and B014 or B018 would become the better choice. I do not hold that criterion, but I accept it is a legitimate one.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube first and the clock fifth to B009, but warns that unanimity and breadth of support should not be mistaken for depth of scientific weight, and notes that the clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own.
responses.response: I take the warning seriously, and I think it is right that the committee should not count rankings as evidence. But I would partly dispute the claim that nothing has been delivered. The gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample and the intercomparison bounds on constant variation are results about nature that only this class of clock could give, even if no new particle or field has been found. I would concede that the dark-matter and geodesy cases are projections. So my answer to his question is that the weight is real but concentrated in two delivered results and in the invention itself, not spread across the full list of advertised applications, and the citation should not claim more than that. I also note that his own move came from the attribution argument, which is a scientific-credit argument and not a headcount.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, now prefers B009 and regards IceCube as the best alternative, but says source identification is still at moderate significance and that credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors is hard to settle.
responses.response: IceCube is outside my field, and he is better placed than I am to judge the instrument history, so I defer to him on the facts. His own admission is, in effect, the argument I made in round 1: a prize that cannot decide between the 2013 diffuse flux, the concept of the detector and the later source identifications will have a harder citation to write than Katori and Ye. If the committee wanted a discovery-class prize this year, I would want him to say in the room which two names he would defend for Halzen and Karle versus Spiering, and what the citation would credit. Without that, I would not move B052 above B009, though I agree it is a serious candidate for a later year when source association is firmer.

responses.point: Kroll supports B009, discloses his research period in the Hall laboratory where Ye trained, and argues the comb and ion-clock lineage should be handled by citation wording rather than by widening the prize; he also lists waiting for the redefinition of the second as a risk.
responses.response: I agree on the wording point: the comb is the clockwork and the ion trap is another route to accuracy, whereas the invention here is magic-wavelength confinement of neutral atoms, so a citation that says so addresses the overlap better than adding names, which the three-person limit would anyway not allow for the Sr, Yb and Hg groups. On his disclosed connection, I think the right treatment is recording it, as he did, not recusal, since it is a training tie and not a stake, and the case does not depend on his vote. I would add that Ye's independent accuracy results stand regardless of that lineage. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree mildly with the timing worry for the reason given above.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B009 from B041 and B009 fifth, and says B009 would drop if the committee prefers a prize that changes what physicists can think about over one that changes what they can measure.
responses.response: I think his conditional is the honest statement of where the disagreement lies, and I accept that the choice between a measurement prize and a new-question prize is a value judgment, not a fact. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice does change what can be asked, because it makes it possible to treat a clock as a many-body quantum system and to compare it across height and distance at a level where gravity and constants enter. I would not put it in the same class as topological phases in that respect, and B018 remains a legitimate alternative to him, but I find the clock's attribution cleaner.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B009 with a citation that names magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms but not precision or 1e-18, and keeps B017 as a secondary alternative.
responses.response: I would keep the 1e-18 figure in the citation alongside magic-wavelength trapping, because it states what the realisation achieved and answers the question of why this is more than a wavelength trick. Her objection is probably that a number can be overtaken, a point Eriksson also raised, and I accept it: the phrase should read as the level reached, not as a standing record. I agree with her treatment of B017: it is mature, but the STEM corrector credit is a known gap.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as discovery-class when the strongest delivered results are bounds and redshift measurements rather than a new particle or phase.
Whether a third precision atomic-physics prize in about twenty years is acceptable for the balance of fields.
Whether a two-name citation can state clearly enough what it does not credit (Sr, Yb and Hg groups elsewhere, ion clocks, combs) without sounding dismissive of them.
My own recall of the priority history of the first lattice-clock demonstrations is from memory and not verified here.
I cannot tell how the committee will react if the redefinition of the second is decided in either direction before the vote.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT at Chalmers and work on superconducting circuits, so B008 (circuit QED) lies in my own field and I would recuse on any decision that turns on it; I have dropped it from my alternatives for that reason. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum are documented links to the circuit field, and Chalmers hosted researchers tied to the 2025 prize. I have no apparent connection to Katori, Ye or the other B009 contributors, nor to B014 or B018. I note that the chair summary mentions Olsson listing me as a Chalmers colleague; I have no further connection to disclose on that point.
